metadata.title: Recurring Decimals and Fraction Conversion
metadata.description: Recognize repeating decimals and convert pure or mixed recurring decimals into fractions.
metadata.teachingApproach: Teach through short, connected phone-sized screens: a concrete idea, worked steps on separate lines, a reason and check, then fresh practice. Wrong answers receive a worked correction and a parallel retry that must be answered correctly before the lesson advances.
metadata.sourceScope: R.S. Aggarwal, Quantitative Aptitude for Competitive Examinations, Chapter 3: recurring-decimal definitions and conversion rules on printed page 70; solved examples 17-18 on printed pages 72-73; objective patterns on recurring-to-fraction conversion in the chapter exercise and answer section.

content.text:
Let's understand decimals that never end but follow a pattern.

In 0.3333…, the digit 3 keeps repeating. We write it as 0.(3). Parentheses show exactly which digits repeat, so we can turn the decimal into an exact fraction.

A terminating decimal stops, like 0.375. A recurring decimal has a repeating digit or block that continues forever.

0.(34) means 0.343434… . The block 34 starts immediately after the point, so this is a pure recurring decimal.

0.2(7) means 0.27777… . The 2 appears once; only 7 repeats. Because the repeat begins after a non-repeating prefix, this is mixed recurring.

Parentheses are part of the meaning. Without a repeat mark, 0.27 is simply a terminating decimal.
Which number is a pure recurring decimal?

inlineData.prompt: Which number is a pure recurring decimal?
hints: Pure means the repeat begins immediately after the point.
Only one choice marks an infinite repeating block.
inlineData.explanation: 0.(45) means 0.454545…; the repeating block starts at the first decimal place. The other written decimals terminate.

content.text:
Look for parentheses around the repeat block or an explicit ellipsis. 0.375 ends and is terminating; 0.(45) repeats 45 from the first decimal place and is pure recurring.

0.(45) means 0.454545…; the repeating block starts at the first decimal place. The other written decimals terminate.

Use the same idea with a new set of values.
Which decimal is terminating?

inlineData.prompt: Which decimal is terminating?
hints: A terminating decimal has finitely many digits and no continuing repeat.
Read the parentheses as an instruction that the marked digits recur forever.
inlineData.explanation: 0.625 is a finite decimal. The other choices indicate repeating digits.

content.text:
Let’s check this one.

A terminating decimal has finitely many digits and no continuing repeat.

0.625 is a finite decimal. The other choices indicate repeating digits.

Try the same question again and check the result.

The repeating block is called the period.

0.(27) repeats 27, a two-digit block:
0.272727…

0.2(8) repeats only 8:
0.288888…

Those decimals are different even though their first two written digits follow a similar pattern.

Read the parentheses before counting the period. The number of digits in the period will decide how many 9s appear in its fraction denominator.
In 0.2(7), which part repeats?

inlineData.prompt: In 0.2(7), which part repeats?
hints: The bar is placed over the digit 7 only.
The 2 before it is a non-repeating prefix.
inlineData.explanation: The decimal means 0.2777…: 2 is the prefix and 7 repeats.

content.text:
Read the parentheses carefully: 0.(27) has a two-digit period, 27. In 0.2(7), the prefix is 2 and the one-digit period is 7.

The decimal means 0.2777…: 2 is the prefix and 7 repeats.

Use the same idea with a new set of values.
How many digits are in the repeating block of 0.(142)?

inlineData.prompt: How many digits are in the repeating block of 0.(142)?
hints: Count the digits inside the parentheses.

content.text:
Let’s check this one.

Count the digits inside the parentheses.

The period 142 has three digits.

Try the same question again and check the result.

Why does a repeating 6 become a fraction over 9? Let x = 0.(6) = 0.6666… .

Multiply by 10. One repeated digit moves before the point:
10x = 6.6666…

Now subtract the original x:

10x − x = 6.6666… − 0.6666…
9x = 6, so x = 6/9 = 2/3.

The endless tails match and cancel. That is why a one-digit pure repeat uses 9 in the denominator.
Convert 0.(8) to a fraction in lowest terms.

inlineData.prompt: Convert 0.(8) to a fraction in lowest terms.
hints: Let x = 0.888… and compare 10x with x.
inlineData.explanation: 9x = 8, so x = 8/9, already in lowest terms.

content.text:
If x = 0.666…, then 10x = 6.666…. Subtracting gives 9x = 6, so x = 6/9 = 2/3.

9x = 8, so x = 8/9, already in lowest terms.

Use the same idea with a new set of values.
Convert 0.(3) to a fraction in lowest terms.

inlineData.prompt: Convert 0.(3) to a fraction in lowest terms.

content.text:
Let’s check this one.

Subtract x = 0.333… from 10x = 3.333… .

9x = 3, so x = 3/9 = 1/3.

Try the same question again and check the result.

For a two-digit block, shift two places. Let x = 0.(36) = 0.363636… .

Then 100x = 36.363636… . The repeating tails now match those in x.

Subtract:

100x − x = 36
99x = 36
x = 36/99 = 4/11.

Two digits in the period give two 9s. Reduce only after writing the correct fraction. A one-digit shift would leave the tails unmatched.
Convert 0.(27) to a fraction in lowest terms.

inlineData.prompt: Convert 0.(27) to a fraction in lowest terms.
hints: The period has two digits, so compare 100x and x.
The first fraction is 27/99; reduce it.

content.text:
For x = 0.272727…, multiply by 100 because the block has two digits. Then 100x − x = 27, so 99x = 27 and x = 27/99 = 3/11.

99x = 27, hence x = 27/99 = 3/11.

Use the same idea with a new set of values.
Convert 0.(142) to a fraction.

inlineData.prompt: Convert 0.(142) to a fraction.
inlineData.explanation: For a pure three-digit period, 0.(142) = 142/999. This fraction is already reduced.

content.text:
Let’s check this one.

The three-digit period produces three 9s.

For a pure three-digit period, 0.(142) = 142/999. This fraction is already reduced.

Try the same question again and check the result.

A period can begin with zero. In 0.(042), the full block is 042:

0.042042042…

It has three digits, even though its first digit is zero.

So the denominator has three 9s:

0.(042) = 42/999 = 14/333.

Do not use 42/99; that would mean 0.(42), a different decimal. Check the first digits of the fraction's decimal expansion against the written block.
Convert 0.(067) to a fraction.

inlineData.prompt: Convert 0.(067) to a fraction.
hints: The repeated block is 067, which has three places.
inlineData.explanation: The block 067 gives numerator 67 and denominator 999: 67/999.

content.text:
Count all digits inside the parentheses, including the leading zero. The block 067 has length three, so use denominator 999: 67/999.

The block 067 gives numerator 67 and denominator 999: 67/999.

Use the same idea with a new set of values.
What denominator structure is used for the pure repeat 0.(004)?

inlineData.prompt: What denominator structure is used for the pure repeat 0.(004)?
hints: Count the three digits in 004, including the zeroes.
inlineData.explanation: The period 004 has three digits, so its denominator is 999; the fraction is 4/999.

content.text:
Let’s check this one.

Count the three digits in 004, including the zeroes.

The period 004 has three digits, so its denominator is 999; the fraction is 4/999.

Try the same question again and check the result.

Now let one digit appear once before the repeat: x = 0.2(7) = 0.2777… .

One shift removes the non-repeating prefix:
10x = 2.7777… .

Shift one more place to move a full repeating digit:
100x = 27.7777… .

Subtract matching tails:
100x − 10x = 27 − 2
90x = 25
x = 25/90 = 5/18.

The 9 comes from the repeating digit; the 0 comes from the prefix.
Convert 0.1(6) to a fraction in lowest terms.

inlineData.prompt: Convert 0.1(6) to a fraction in lowest terms.

content.text:
For 0.1666…, subtract the shifted values 16.666… − 1.666… = 15. Thus 90x = 15 and x = 1/6.

The prefix-and-repeat rule gives (16 − 1)/90 = 15/90 = 1/6.

Use the same idea with a new set of values.
Convert 0.2(3) to a fraction in lowest terms.

inlineData.prompt: Convert 0.2(3) to a fraction in lowest terms.

content.text:
Let’s check this one.

Use (23 − 2)/90.

(23 − 2)/90 = 21/90 = 7/30.

Try the same question again and check the result.

In 0.14(6), the prefix 14 does not repeat; only 6 does.

Build the numerator from the digits through one full repeat, then subtract the prefix:
146 − 14 = 132.

Use one 9 for the one-digit repeat and two zeros for the two-digit prefix:

0.14(6) = 132/900 = 11/75.

Check size: 11/75 is between 0.14 and 0.15, matching 0.14666… . The zeros record how far the repeat begins after the point.
Convert 0.23(4) to a fraction.

inlineData.prompt: Convert 0.23(4) to a fraction.
hints: One repeat digit and two prefix digits give denominator 900.

content.text:
There are two prefix digits and one repeating digit. Compute (234 − 23)/(9 followed by 2 zeroes) = 211/900.

(234 − 23)/900 = 211/900, already in lowest terms.

Use the same idea with a new set of values.
Convert 0.12(3) to a fraction in lowest terms.

inlineData.prompt: Convert 0.12(3) to a fraction in lowest terms.

content.text:
Let’s check this one.

Use (123 − 12)/900.

(123 − 12)/900 = 111/900 = 37/300.

Try the same question again and check the result.

Now look at 0.4(12) = 0.4121212… . The prefix is 4; the period is 12.

Take the digits through one full period, 412, and subtract the prefix, 4:
412 − 4 = 408.

Two repeating digits give 99; one prefix digit adds a 0:

0.4(12) = 408/990 = 68/165.

Check the size: about 0.412. Count the period and prefix separately so that you do not accidentally treat 412 as the repeating block.
Convert 0.2(35) to a fraction.

inlineData.prompt: Convert 0.2(35) to a fraction.

content.text:
The prefix has one digit and the period has two. Subtract 2 from 235 and use denominator 990: 233/990.

(235 − 2)/990 = 233/990.

Use the same idea with a new set of values.
Convert 1.2(3) to an improper fraction.

inlineData.prompt: Convert 1.2(3) to an improper fraction.
inlineData.explanation: Separate the whole part: 1.2(3) = 1 + 0.2(3). The recurring part is (23 − 2)/90 = 7/30. Thus the total is 1 + 7/30 = 37/30.

content.text:
Keep the whole 1 separate.

0.2(3) = (23 − 2)/90 = 7/30, so 1.2(3) = 1 + 7/30 = 37/30. Try this conversion again.

A whole-number part can be handled separately. For 2.(36), first convert the decimal part:

0.(36) = 36/99 = 4/11.

Put the 2 back:

2 + 4/11 = 26/11.

Check: 26/11 = 2.363636… = 2.(36). Reducing a fraction does not change its value, but forgetting the whole number does.
Convert 2.(45) to an improper fraction.

inlineData.prompt: Convert 2.(45) to an improper fraction.

content.text:
Separate 3.(142857) as 3 + 0.(142857). The recurring part is 142857/999999 = 1/7, so the total is 3 + 1/7 = 22/7.

2.(45) = 2 + 45/99 = 2 + 5/11 = 27/11.

Use the same idea with a new set of values.
Convert 3.(27) to an improper fraction.

inlineData.prompt: Convert 3.(27) to an improper fraction.

content.text:
Let’s check this one.

0.(27) = 27/99 = 3/11.

3 + 3/11 = 33/11 + 3/11 = 36/11.

Try the same question again and check the result.

A converted fraction should reproduce the repeating pattern. For example:

0.(3) = 1/3
0.(27) = 27/99 = 3/11.

Dividing 3 by 11 begins 0.2727…, which checks the period.

Fractions also make comparisons exact. For example, 0.(7) = 7/9 = 77/99, while 0.(68) = 68/99.

Since 77/99 > 68/99, we know 0.(7) > 0.(68). Compare their values, not only the first displayed digit.
Which recurring decimal is greater: 0.(6) or 0.(61)?

inlineData.prompt: Which recurring decimal is greater: 0.(6) or 0.(61)?

content.text:
Convert each pure recurring decimal exactly: 0.(6) = 6/9 = 2/3 = 66/99, and 0.(61) = 61/99. Since 66/99 > 61/99, 0.(6) is greater.

0.(6) = 2/3 = 66/99, while 0.(61) = 61/99. Thus 0.(6) is greater.

Use the same idea with a new set of values.
Evaluate 0.(6) + 0.(1) as an exact fraction.

inlineData.prompt: Evaluate 0.(6) + 0.(1) as an exact fraction.
hints: Convert the pure repeats to 6/9 and 1/9.

content.text:
Let’s check this one.

Convert the pure repeats to 6/9 and 1/9.

0.(6) = 2/3 = 6/9; 0.(1) = 1/9. Their sum is 7/9.

Try the same question again and check the result.

You can read the exact repeat block and convert pure or mixed recurring decimals into fractions.

Count repeating digits for the 9s and prefix digits for the 0s. Reduce the fraction, then divide or estimate to check that its opening digits match the original decimal.
